The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

vignette: As he walked through the fields, checking on his crops, Amir couldn't shake off the feeling of unease that had been plaguing him for months. It was a sensation that started in his chest, a tightness that seemed to spread throughout his body like a slow-moving fire. His heart would start racing, pounding against his ribcage, and he could feel the sweat beading on his forehead, mixing with the dirt and grime of the day's work. It had been six months since the assault, but the memories still felt like they belonged to someone else. Amir couldn't quite piece together what had happened that night - fragments would flash in his mind, disconnected and disjointed: a hand on his shoulder, a voice whispering in his ear, the sound of footsteps crunching on gravel. But when he tried to explain it all to his wife, or even just to himself, the words got tangled up and he couldn't finish the story. Amir's wife had been worried about him, noticed how he'd been throwing himself into work, trying to keep his mind occupied with the never-ending tasks of running a farm. But Amir knew that wasn't the real reason - he was just trying to avoid thinking about it all. He avoided anniversaries, too - dates and times that connected back to that night - because they made him feel like he was reliving it all over again. As he worked, Amir's mind would wander to thoughts of revenge. He'd ruminate on ways to get even with his assailant, fantasies that felt satisfying in the moment but left him feeling hollow afterwards. His wife had tried to reassure him that the police were doing their job, that justice would be served - but Amir couldn't shake off the feeling that it wasn't enough. He was constantly on edge, too, always scanning his surroundings for signs of potential threats. People acting suspiciously made him tense up, ready to defend himself at a moment's notice. He'd see someone lingering around the farm and his mind would start racing - who were they? What did they want? The smell of sweat or body odor would transport him back to that night, too. It was like his senses had been hijacked, taking him on a journey through memories he couldn't quite grasp. Amir's wife had finally convinced him to seek help when she noticed how withdrawn he'd become - how he stopped attending community events, stopped spending time with friends and family. He knew he needed to get better, not just for himself but for the people who loved him. As he sat in his therapist's office, describing all this, Amir felt a sense of relief wash over him. For the first time in months, he allowed himself to feel a glimmer of hope - maybe he could learn to live with what had happened, rather than just trying to survive it. But even as he began to open up about his experiences, Amir couldn't shake off the feeling that he was still stuck in that night, trapped in a cycle of fear and anger. What frightened him most was that he might never be able to truly escape - that those memories would haunt him forever, fragmented pieces that refused to cohere into a narrative he could understand.
